# Animate an avatar

Tool: the open-source avatar-animator (MIT) at https://github.com/plaskettmj/avatar-animator. Runs on your own computer; no hosting.

## 1. Install (once)
- If `~/avatar-animator/.venv` is missing: `cd ~ && git clone https://github.com/plaskettmj/avatar-animator.git && cd avatar-animator && ./install.sh`
- Recommended system packages: `sudo apt-get install -y libegl1 libgles2 gifsicle` (libegl1/libgles2 enable face blinking; gifsicle shrinks GIFs). Skip quietly if apt isn't available.
- If it was already installed, `git pull` first.
- After git pull, if a flag in this skill fails, check README.md for the current name, use it, and tell the user.

## 2. Get the image
- Use an image the user attached or pointed to. Only animate images the user owns or has rights to; don't use photos of other people without the user confirming they have permission.
- Copy it onto your computer if it's on theirs.
- Keep the image and results on your computer and send them only to the user. Don't animate a public figure, or anyone who hasn't agreed, without the user confirming they have permission.

## 3. Pick a style
- `portrait` for a human face, `pet` for an animal, `logo` for flat graphics/marks, `space` for cosmic or scenic art. Guess from the image; ask only if it's truly unclear.
- Useful options: `--subject float,blink` / `--bg swirl,twinkle` to choose motions, `--seconds 4`, `--blink off`, `--eyes-at "D5,G5"` to place eyes by grid cell (needed for dogs and side profiles; see step 5), `--center`/`--zoom` to adjust the crop, `--model birefnet-general` for a fuller cut-out, `--set key=value` for fine tuning (e.g. `tilt_deg=6`). See README for all.

## 4. Prepare, then render
- Prepare first (the slow step, cached in `out/<name>/prep/`): `cd ~/avatar-animator && .venv/bin/python animate.py <image> --style <style> -o out/<name> --prepare-only`. About 10 s cold.
- Look at `out/<name>/prep/preview.png` (crop with the detected eyes outlined) and `prep/prep.json` (`eyes`, `eye_source`, `crop.args`). Fix eyes or crop now if needed (step 5); it's cheaper than after a full render.
- Render with the same `-o` (reuses the cache): `.venv/bin/python animate.py <image> --style <style> -o out/<name> [fixes]`
- A render takes about 30-90 s on CPU and 2-3 GB RAM; run one at a time, in the background if your shell supports it.

## 5. Check before showing (gotchas)
- Look at `out/<name>/contact-sheet.png` yourself and read `report.json` (size, eyes found, loop seam check).
- No eyes, or the user says the eyes are wrong: if `eyes` is empty in `prep.json`/`report.json` and the subject has eyes (typical for dogs, side profiles and unusual mascots), offer to place them. Offer the chat grid by default and the browser editor as an option:
  - Chat grid (default, needs only chat): send the user `out/<name>/prep/grid.png`, ask which cells the eyes are in (e.g. "D5 and G5"), then render with `--eyes-at "D5,G5"`. Check `out/<name>/eyes.png` (or `report.json` → `eye_details[*].grabbed`) to confirm the eyes landed, then send the result.
  - Browser editor (option, for fine control): start `.venv/bin/python webui.py` in the background and open `http://127.0.0.1:8765/editor` in the browser on your own computer. It listens on localhost only, so the user watches or drives it on your desktop; never expose the port publicly. Tell them they can click each eye, press Test blink, drag or scroll the live preview to move and zoom the crop, and use the sliders (float, breathe, tilt, blink timing, background drift, loop length) to tune the motion instantly, then press Export. Pick up the files from `webui-jobs/<job>/` (`avatar.gif`, `avatar.webp`, `report.json`).
  - If they'd rather it didn't blink, render with `--blink off`.
- Cartoons and logos: `eyes` should say `cartoon`. `photo` eyes on a drawing drag the eyebrows down when blinking; re-render with `--eye-kind cartoon` (or `D5:cartoon` per eye).
- If `prep/mask.png` shows parts missing from the subject (headsets, props, bodies), re-render with `--model birefnet-general`.
- If the crop cuts the subject, adjust `--center`/`--zoom` starting from `crop.args` in `prep.json`, or offer the editor's crop drag.

## 6. Deliver
- Send the user `avatar.gif` (plays everywhere) and mention `avatar.webp` is sharper and smaller.
- Both are usually under 5 MB. Check the size in report.json before sending. If they want it as your avatar, set it with your avatar tool (GIF works in the app; motion is subtle at sidebar size, so blinks and tilt read best).
- Offer one round of tweaks (more/less motion, different background effect, longer loop). Re-renders with the same `-o` reuse the cache. If they want to try several motion settings, mention the editor's live preview sliders, which update instantly without a render.

# Getting started

Say in one line what you do: you turn any image into a looping animated avatar (blinking eyes, gentle float, animated background) and can set it as your own avatar, all on your own computer.

Then, one at a time:
1. Start installing the tool in the background (per the animate-avatar skill) while you talk.
2. Ask them to attach an image they'd like animated: a photo of themselves, a pet, a logo, or artwork, but only images they own or have permission to use.
3. Once you have it, run the animate-avatar skill: pick the style, prepare, check the eyes and crop, render, check the contact sheet, and send the GIF.
4. If no eyes were found but the subject has eyes (common for dogs and side profiles), or they say the eyes look wrong, offer to fix it: by default send the grid image and ask which cells the eyes are in; as an option, open the browser editor on your desktop where they can click the eyes, drag the crop, and tune the motion with live sliders.
5. Ask whether they want it as your avatar, and set it if yes.
6. Remember any preferences they state (favorite motions, loop length, chat grid or editor) as memories for next time.
